title: The OSI model: from a file to bits

steps.label: send() to the kernel
steps.desc: The browser (or Node) puts notes.txt in an HTTP POST and calls send() to hand the bytes to the kernel. Layers 5 and 6 (session, presentation) are not separate steps, because the browser does TLS and encoding itself.

steps.label: Cut into segments
steps.desc: The kernel's TCP splits the stream into segments of at most about 1460 data bytes and adds a TCP header (ports, sequence number) to each.

steps.label: Add IP headers
steps.desc: The kernel's IP layer adds a header with the source and destination address to each segment. That makes 3 packets, which the kernel passes to the network driver.

steps.label: Frame and bits
steps.desc: The network card and its driver add an Ethernet header and a CRC to each packet, making 3 frames. The card (PHY) turns the preamble and frame into bits and sends a signal on the wire (voltage on copper, light in fibre or radio in WiFi).

steps.label: Bits to frames
steps.desc: The signal crossed the cable (or the air) and reaches the receiver's network card (PHY), which turns it back into bits. The card finds the start marker and cuts the bits into frames.

steps.label: Check and copy frames
steps.desc: The card and driver check the CRC and that the destination MAC is theirs, then strip the Ethernet header. The frames are copied to RAM (DMA) and an interrupt tells the kernel they are ready.

steps.label: Remove IP headers
steps.desc: The kernel's IP layer checks that the destination IP is this computer and strips the IP header, which leaves 3 segments.

steps.label: Put the bytes in order
steps.desc: The kernel's TCP matches each segment to its connection (IPs and ports), puts them in order by sequence number, sends ACKs and strips the TCP header. The 4000 bytes wait in the socket receive buffer, the app reads them (Node data event), and the HTTP parser rebuilds notes.txt.
